section_title: Must Gentile believers become Jews to be saved?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 Then some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.” 2 And after engaging these men in sharp debate, Paul and Barnabas were appointed, along with some other believers, to go up to Jerusalem to see the apostles and elders about this question. 3 Sent on their way by the church, they passed through Phoenicia and Samaria, recounting the conversion of the Gentiles and bringing great joy to all the brothers. 4 On their arrival in Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and apostles and elders, to whom they reported all that God had done through them. 5 But some believers from the party of the Pharisees stood up and declared, “The Gentiles must be circumcised and required to obey the law of Moses.”

6 So the apostles and elders met to look into this matter. 7 After much discussion, Peter got up and said to them, “Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you that the Gentiles would hear from my lips the message of the gospel and believe. 8 And God, who knows the heart, showed His approval by giving the Holy Spirit to them, just as He did to us. 9 He made no distinction between us and them, for He cleansed their hearts by faith. 10 Now then, why do you test God by placing on the necks of the disciples a yoke that neither we nor our fathers have been able to bear? 11 On the contrary, we believe it is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are.”

context_lines: Some men from Judea teach the believers in Antioch that circumcision according to Moses is necessary for salvation. Paul and Barnabas strongly oppose this teaching. The church sends them and others to Jerusalem to discuss the question with the apostles and elders.

The journey brings encouragement to believers in Phoenicia and Samaria as they hear about Gentile conversions. In Jerusalem, the visitors are welcomed and report God’s work. Some believers from the Pharisees’ party then insist that the Gentiles must be circumcised and obey the law of Moses.

After much discussion, Peter points back to what God has already done among the Gentiles. God gave them the Holy Spirit and cleansed their hearts by faith, making no distinction between them and Jewish believers. Peter calls the added requirement a yoke, a burden that neither their ancestors nor they have been able to bear.

He concludes by placing both groups on the same ground: salvation through the grace of the Lord Jesus. Luke describes a serious question within the believing community, not merely a dispute between Christians and outsiders.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly understand Peter’s conclusion as rejecting circumcision and adoption of the Mosaic law as conditions Gentiles must meet to be saved. Jews and Gentiles alike depend on Jesus’ grace, rather than one group entering through a superior national standing.
god_plan_lines: Peter himself connects this decision with the gift of the Spirit in [Acts 10:44–48](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/10.htm). The church must reckon with the fact that God has already received Gentiles; its decision is not what first makes God willing to receive them.

[Galatians 2:15–16](https://biblehub.com/bsb/galatians/2.htm) expresses the related point that both Jewish and Gentile believers are put right with God through faith in Christ rather than works of the law. That connection concerns the gospel itself, without requiring every detail of the visits described in the two books to be fitted into one proposed chronology.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
